survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 microdata for the United States and constructs an analytic sample of complete cases after downloading the OECD PISA 2012 database. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight procedure, and it instead relies on listwise deletion due to missingness in the SEM software. Because the analysis is conducted with AMOS path analysis (SEM/path models) rather than ML algorithms, the paper does not discuss complex survey design adjustments (stratification/clustering) or which PISA weight variable (e.g., student design weights) would be used. For replication, analysts should use the official PISA 2012 student weights and appropriate variance estimation if available, and then re-estimate the path models to assess sensitivity to weighting and missing-data handling.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The authors downloaded an initial set of N=4978 cases from the OECD PISA 2012 downloadable database for the United States. Missing (incomplete) data prompted the SEM software to use listwise deletion, yielding a complete-data analytic sample of N=2968. The outcome mathematics achievement was computed as the average of the first three plausible mathematics achievement values for each student, and the same complete-case sample was used across all path models to facilitate comparisons.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 (United States) — Mathematics achievement (Grade 7th or equivalent, 15-year-olds)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics achievement (average of first three plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Path model fit: chi-square p < .01; NFI/CFI ≈ .95/.93 (meets or nearly meets .95 threshold); RMSEA < .05 for Fig. 1. Standardized direct effects (α = .01): SESHP → Math = .31 SD; Parent education → Math = .09 SD; Teacher support → Math = .10 SD. Standardized indirect effects (Table 4): Parent education → Math via SESHP/occupation/teacher support = .20 SD; SESHP indirect via teacher support = -.06 SD; Teacher support indirect via parent occupation = -.01 SD.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 (United States) the study leveraged Mother and father education, SES + home possessions (SESHP), Teacher support, and Parent occupation status to model mathematics achievement (average of the first three plausible values) in a path analysis, finding that SESHP had the largest positive direct association with mathematics achievement (.31 SD) and that Parent education also showed a substantial positive indirect effect (.20 SD) beyond bivariate correlations. This indicates that SES-related resources operate through multiple pathways (home material capital and social capital from teachers), so SES measurement and reporting should consider indirect mechanisms rather than relying only on direct SES–achievement associations.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2012 microdata for the United States (analytic N=2,968 after listwise deletion of missing cases) to examine how socio-economic status (SES) relates to mathematics achievement through direct and indirect pathways using path analysis in AMOS. Mathematics achievement is computed as the average of the first three plausible mathematics achievement values for each student, and the authors report model fit indices (chi-square p<.01; NFI/CFI around .95/.93; RMSEA <.05 for the simpler model and ~.08 for the more complex model). In the simpler model, SESHP shows the largest direct effect on mathematics achievement (.31 SD), and parent education has a sizable positive indirect effect (.20 SD). In the more complex model, PISA SES has the strongest direct effect (.32 SD) and multiple indirect effects suggest SES influences achievement via home possessions and teacher support/relations. Limitations include the use of complete cases (potential bias if data are not missing at random) and the absence of reported survey-weight handling.
